Starts with smallestEvenIndex = -1 (meaning “none found yet”).

Loops through values[0..length-1].

For each even element (values[i] % 2 == 0), if it’s the first even seen or it’s smaller than the current smallest even, remember its index.

After the loop, if an even number was found, printf("%d", smallestEvenIndex);.

Details/edge cases:

If there are no even numbers, it prints nothing.

If there are ties for the smallest even value, it prints the first such index (uses <, not <=).

Zero counts as even; negative evens are allowed (e.g., −4 is considered, and may be the smallest).

No newline is printed.

Goal: find the smallest even number in the array and print all indices where it occurs, printed from right to left.

“Even” means divisible by 2 (including 0 and negative evens like -4).

How it works

Scan left → right to find the smallest even value

smallestEven starts at -1 as a sentinel meaning “not found yet.”

For each element, if it is even and either no even has been found yet or it’s smaller than the current smallestEven, update smallestEven and remember its index in smallestEvenIndex (this index is later unused).

If no even numbers exist

If smallestEven is still -1, it prints No evens followed by a newline and returns.

Print all positions of that smallest even (right → left)

Loop from the end of the array down to the start.

For each position where values[i] == smallestEven, print the index with printf("%d ", i);.

Note: prints a trailing space and no newline after the indices.

Behavior notes / edge cases

If there are multiple copies of the smallest even, it prints all their indices in descending order (e.g., indices 7 4 2 ).

If there is one smallest even, it prints just that index (e.g., 3 ).

If the array is empty (length == 0), it prints No evens.

It finds the mathematically smallest value, so among {-4, 2}, -4 is chosen.

Time complexity: O(n) (two linear scans). Extra memory: O(1).
